subtopics.title: Moral and Ethical Factors and Implications of the Use of IT

comparisonTable.title: Key Ethical Issues in IT — Overview
rows: Privacy
Right to control personal data; risk of surveillance/data misuse
Social media tracking browsing history for ads
All individuals using digital systems
Environmental Impact
IT causes e-waste, energy consumption, carbon emissions
Data centres consuming ~1% of global electricity
Society, environment, future generations
Unequal Access
Digital divide — not everyone can afford/access technology
Rural areas with no broadband; low-income households without devices
Disadvantaged communities, developing nations
Assistive Tech Access
Disabled users need assistive technologies but access is unequal
Screen readers cost hundreds; not all employers provide them
Disabled users, employers, schools
Online Behaviour
Netiquette and responsible digital communication
Cyberbullying, trolling, spreading misinformation online
All users, especially young people
Acceptable Use Policies
Organisational rules governing IT use by staff/students
School AUP banning social media on school devices
Employees, students, organisations

items.definition: A person's right to control how their personal information is collected, used and shared.
items.examples: Apps tracking your location for adverts; employers monitoring staff emails.
items.examTip: Weigh individual rights against organisations' interests, and cite GDPR/DPA 2018.
keyFacts: Collect only the data you need

items.definition: The effect of IT on the environment: energy use, e-waste and emissions from manufacturing.
items.examples: Data centres using 1–2% of the world's electricity; toxic e-waste.
items.examTip: Give both sides: energy and e-waste vs less travel, paperless offices and smart grids.
keyFacts: E-waste is the fastest-growing waste stream
Devices need rare metals mined at a high cost
Cloud can be more efficient than many small servers

items.definition: The digital divide: the gap between people who have devices, internet and skills and those who don't.
items.examples: Rural areas without fast broadband; elderly people shut out of online services.
items.examTip: Three gaps: access (no device or internet), skills, and usage.
keyFacts: Linked to income, location, age and education
Millions of UK adults lack basic digital skills

items.definition: Whether disabled people get fair access to the assistive technology they need.
items.examples: An employer not providing a screen reader; a website that fails accessibility standards.
items.examTip: Ethical AND legal: the Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments.

items.definition: Standards of respectful behaviour online, avoiding harm such as cyberbullying and trolling.
items.examples: Cyberbullying on social media; spreading false rumours about a business.
items.examTip: Netiquette is informal; an AUP is the formal version. Cover anonymity and impact on victims.
keyFacts: Netiquette: be polite, no ALL CAPS, cite sources

items.definition: A written agreement setting out what users may and may not do on an organisation's IT systems.
items.examples: A school banning gaming on its laptops; a company banning shared logins.
items.examTip: Contents: allowed uses, banned activities, monitoring, and consequences of breaking it.
keyFacts: Users cannot claim they didn't know the rules
Should say that activity may be monitored

subtopics.title: Role and Impact of Current Legislation in Protecting IT Systems, Users and Their Data

comparisonTable.title: UK IT Legislation — Summary Comparison
rows: Computer Misuse Act
1990 (amended)
Unauthorised access to computer systems and data
S1: Unauthorised access; S2: Unauthorised access with intent; S3: Unauthorised modification
S1: 2 yrs; S2: 5 yrs; S3: 10 yrs imprisonment
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act
Intellectual property rights for creative works and software
Reproducing/distributing copyrighted work without permission
Civil damages + up to 10 years imprisonment for criminal infringement
Copyright (Computer Programs) Regulations
Specific IP protection for software and programs
Copying, reverse engineering, or distributing software illegally
Same as CDPA 1988
Health & Safety / DSE Regulations
Workplace safety for IT/screen users
Employers must provide DSE assessments, breaks, training, proper equipment
Civil claims / HSE enforcement
Data Protection Act / UK GDPR
Protection of personal data; rights of data subjects
Unlawful processing, failure to report breaches, inadequate security
ICO fines up to £17.5m or 4% global turnover

items.definition: Makes it illegal to access computers without permission or to misuse them to commit crime.
items.examples: Hacking a database (S1); hacking to commit fraud (S2); spreading ransomware (S3).
items.examTip: Know the sections: S1 access only; S2 access with intent to commit more crime; S3 damaging or changing systems.

comparisonTable.title: Computer Misuse Act 1990 — Three Offences
rows: Section 1
Unauthorised access to computer material
Using someone else's password to log into their account out of curiosity
2 years imprisonment + unlimited fine
Section 2
Unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences
Hacking into a bank's system intending to transfer funds fraudulently
5 years imprisonment + unlimited fine
Section 3
Unauthorised acts with intent to impair operation of a computer
Deploying ransomware; launching a DDoS attack; installing a keylogger
10 years imprisonment + unlimited fine

keyFacts: S2: with intent to commit further crime (up to 5 years)
S3: unauthorised modification, e.g. malware or DDoS (up to 10 years)

items.definition: Protects creators' work, including software, from being copied or shared without permission.
items.examples: Copying software without a licence; sharing pirated films.
items.examTip: Software counts as a literary work; piracy is a crime, and employers can be liable.
keyFacts: Copyright is automatic in the UK
Licences (EULAs) set how software may be used
Limited exceptions for study and review

items.definition: Regulations that specifically protect computer programs as literary works.
items.examples: Copying another company's source code and selling it as your own.
items.examTip: Adds to the 1988 Act for software: a backup copy is allowed; decompiling only for compatibility.
keyFacts: Owners may make one backup copy

items.term: Health and Safety and Display Screen Equipment (DSE) Regulations
items.definition: Laws requiring employers to protect staff who use computer screens regularly.
items.examples: Providing an adjustable chair, eye tests and screen breaks.
items.examTip: Employer duties: assess workstations, allow breaks, pay for eye tests, give training.

comparisonTable.title: DSE Regulations — Employer Obligations vs Health Risks Addressed
rows: Workstation risk assessment (screen, keyboard, chair, lighting, space)
Musculoskeletal disorders — RSI, back/neck pain from poor posture
Regular breaks from DSE work (at least 5-10 mins per hour)
Eye strain, headaches, fatigue from prolonged screen use
Free eye tests for DSE workers (annually or as needed)
Visual fatigue, uncorrected vision problems worsened by screen work
Provide corrective glasses if required specifically for DSE work
Vision deterioration linked directly to screen use
Training on safe workstation setup and correct posture
Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI), carpal tunnel syndrome from poor technique
Report DSE-related illness under RIDDOR if absence > 7 days
Work-related upper limb disorder (WRULD) — employer accountability

keyFacts: Prevents back pain, eye strain and RSI

items.term: Data Protection Legislation (Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR)
items.definition: The main UK law on how personal data is collected, used, stored and deleted.
items.examples: A GP keeping records accurate and secure; reporting a breach within 72 hours.
items.examTip: Know the principles, people's rights, the ICO's role and the fines.

comparisonTable.title: UK GDPR — Seven Data Protection Principles
rows: 1. Lawfulness, Fairness & Transparency
Data processed legally, fairly, and openly
Collecting location data without informing users
2. Purpose Limitation
Data only used for the specific purpose it was collected for
Using customer purchase data to build psychological profiles for resale
3. Data Minimisation
Only collect data that is necessary
Asking for date of birth when only age range is needed
4. Accuracy
Data must be accurate and kept up to date
Storing outdated address causing important letters to be sent elsewhere
5. Storage Limitation
Data not kept longer than necessary
Retaining old employee records indefinitely after departure
6. Integrity & Confidentiality
Data secured against unauthorised access, loss, or destruction
Storing customer passwords in plaintext; inadequate firewall
7. Accountability
Organisation must demonstrate compliance
No documented data protection policies; no DPO appointed where required

keyFacts: Principles: lawful, set purpose, minimal, accurate, not kept too long, secure
Report serious breaches to the ICO within 72 hours
Fines up to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover
